title.text: Vectors: how AI measures that two pieces of data are alike

objects.text: When an assistant searches your documents, how does it find the passage that fits your question?

Mathematics for AI and Machine Learning  |  Session 2 of 18  |  Linear algebra
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes: Welcome back. Last session we met sums, functions and logarithms. Today we meet vectors, the list of numbers that sits behind every row of data. By the end you will be able to measure how alike two things are with a single number. That is exactly what an AI assistant does when it searches your documents for the passage that answers your question.

title.text: Today in one view: what you will leave with

objects.text: By the end of today you can
Write a row of data as a vector, and add, scale and compare vectors by hand
Calculate the dot product (inner product), the L2 norm, the Euclidean distance and the cosine similarity
Rank six short sentences against a query with cosine similarity, in Python and in a spreadsheet

slides.notes:
By the end of today you can write a row of data as a vector, and add, scale and compare vectors by hand. You can calculate the dot product, which is also called the inner product, the L2 norm, the Euclidean distance and the cosine similarity. And you can rank six short sentences against a query using cosine similarity, in Python and in a spreadsheet.

That last step is a small version of how an AI assistant finds the right passage in your documents.

title.text:
Your two hours: vectors,
then the lab, then AI search

objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: Ideas first. Then the lab, in Python or in a spreadsheet. Then where it shows up in AI.

slides.notes: The first ten minutes recall last session and pose the question of the day. Then thirty-five minutes of ideas, each with a picture and a small calculation by hand, a break, and a forty-five minute lab in Python or in a spreadsheet. The last fifteen minutes show where today appears in AI document search, and give you an exit check. Then you save your work.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  What does the symbol Σ (sigma) mean?
2.  What does the logarithm of a product equal?
3.  Why do AI programs add log-probabilities?

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 1. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. What does the symbol Σ (sigma) mean? Take a moment.

A good answer is this. Add up everything that follows it, from the start index to the stop index.

Question two. What does the logarithm of a product equal? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. The sum of the logarithms: ln(u × v) = ln u + ln v.

Question three. Why do AI programs add log-probabilities? Think about your own task as you answer.

A good answer is this. A product of many small probabilities underflows to 0. A sum of logs stays an ordinary number.

If an answer was missing, do not worry. Your notes from last class have it. Now to today.

title.text: Answers to the three questions from Session 1

rows.text: What does the symbol Σ (sigma) mean?
Add up everything that follows it, from the start index to the stop index.
What does the logarithm of a product equal?
The sum of the logarithms: ln(u × v) = ln u + ln v.
Why do AI programs add log-probabilities?
A product of many small probabilities underflows to 0. A sum of logs stays an ordinary number.

objects.text: If one answer surprised you, look again at the Session 1 slides before the lab.

slides.notes: The short answers first. Sigma means add up everything that follows it, from the start index to the stop index. The logarithm of a product equals the sum of the logarithms. And AI programs add log-probabilities because a product of many small probabilities becomes too small for the computer and rounds to zero, while a sum of logs stays an ordinary number. If you got all three, you are ready for vectors.

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: A list of d numbers in a fixed order. A row of data is a vector. d is its dimension.
Multiply matching entries of two vectors, then add. The result is one number.
The length of a vector: the square root of the sum of its squared entries.
The cosine of the angle between two vectors: 1 for the same direction, 0 at a right angle.
A vector that represents a piece of text so that similar meanings get similar vectors.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Vector. A list of d numbers in a fixed order. A row of data is a vector. d is its dimension.

Dot product (inner product). Multiply matching entries of two vectors, then add. The result is one number.

L2 norm (Euclidean norm). The length of a vector: the square root of the sum of its squared entries.

Cosine similarity. The cosine of the angle between two vectors: 1 for the same direction, 0 at a right angle.

Embedding. A vector that represents a piece of text so that similar meanings get similar vectors.

title.text:
A row of data is a vector: a list
of numbers in a fixed order

objects.alt: A row of data is a vector: a list of numbers in a fixed order

objects.text: Years, hours a week, score of 100: x = (21, 6, 72), d = 3. Written across to save space.

slides.notes:
A table of data has rows, and every row is a vector. Here are three learners, with age, hours studied per week and a quiz score. These numbers are made up. The gold row is Amina, and written as a vector called x it is the list twenty-one, six, seventy-two.

The number of entries is called the dimension, written d, and here d is three. A table with n rows is n vectors. The order matters, so age always comes first. Today I write vectors across the page to save space. In Session 3 they stand up as columns, which is how matrix work writes them.

title.text:
A vector with two numbers is an
arrow from the origin to a point

objects.alt: A vector with two numbers is an arrow from the origin to a point

objects.text: The origin is the point (0, 0). The vector a = (3, 4) is the arrow from the origin to the point 3 across and 4 up.

runs.text: b = (4, 3) is a second vector: 4 across and 3 up.
With 4 or more numbers we cannot draw the arrow, but the rules stay the same.

slides.notes:
With two numbers we can draw a vector. It is an arrow that starts at the origin, the point zero zero, and ends at the point given by the numbers. For a equals three, four, go three across and four up. The red arrow is b, which is four across and three up.

They point in different directions, and we will measure exactly how different in a few slides. With four or more numbers we cannot draw the arrow on paper, but every rule you see today works unchanged in higher dimensions. That matters, because real data often has hundreds of columns.

title.text:
Adding vectors places one
arrow at the tip of the other

objects.alt: Adding vectors places one arrow at the tip of the other

objects.text: Vector addition: add the matching entries. (3, 4) + (4, 3) = (7, 7).

runs.text: Draw b starting at the tip of a. The red arrow from the origin to the end is a + b.
Both vectors must have the same number of entries.

slides.notes:
To add two vectors, add the matching entries. Three plus four is seven, and four plus three is seven, so a plus b is seven, seven. In the picture, draw b starting at the tip of a. The red arrow from the origin to the new tip is the sum.

This works only when both vectors have the same number of entries. Try one, two, three plus ten, ten, ten: the answer is eleven, twelve, thirteen.

title.text:
Scaling a vector by a number
stretches or shrinks the arrow

objects.alt: Scaling a vector by a number stretches or shrinks the arrow

objects.text: Scaling: multiply every entry by one number c, called a scalar. 2 × (3, 4) = (6, 8).

runs.text: A scalar above 1 stretches the arrow. A scalar between 0 and 1 shrinks it.
A positive scalar keeps the direction. A negative scalar reverses it.

slides.notes:
To scale a vector, multiply every entry by one number, called a scalar. Twice three four is six eight. In the picture the red arrow is twice as long as a and points the same way. The grey arrow is half of a. A scalar above one stretches the arrow, and a scalar between zero and one shrinks it.

A negative scalar flips the arrow around, and a positive scalar keeps the direction. Cosine similarity, later today, depends on that fact. What is three times the vector one, two?

title.text:
Vectors add entry by entry, and
a scalar multiplies every entry

objects.alt: Vectors add entry by entry, and a scalar multiplies every entry

rows.text: Two vectors with the same number of entries. Bold letters mean vectors.
Entry 1 and entry 2 of a. The subscript is the position.
A single number, called a scalar.

objects.text: Written across to save space; Session 3 stands vectors up as columns. Python: a + b, 2 * a.

slides.notes:
The two operations as formulas. Bold letters are vectors, and the small numbers are positions. To add, add position by position. To scale, multiply every position by the scalar c. With our numbers, three four plus four three is seven seven, and two times three four is six eight.

In Python you write a plus b and two times a, and numpy does it entry by entry. A vector with two entries cannot be added to one with three, because the third entry has no partner.

title.text:
The dot product multiplies matching
entries and adds the results

objects.alt: The dot product multiplies matching entries and adds the results

objects.text: Dot product (also called inner product): multiply matching entries, then add.

runs.text: The products are 2, 0 and 2, and they add up to 4.
The result is a single number.

slides.notes:
The dot product, also called the inner product, is the most important operation in this course. Take two vectors of the same length. Multiply the entries that sit in the same position, then add the products. For u equals one, two, two and v equals two, zero, one, the products are two, zero and two, and the total is four.

Two vectors go in and one single number comes out. You already know the pattern from Session one, because it is a sigma sum of products. What is the dot product of u with itself?

title.text:
Written with sigma, the dot
product is a sum of d products

objects.alt: Written with sigma, the dot product is a sum of d products

rows.text: Add up over the d entries. d is the number of entries.
Entry i of u and of v.
The dot product: one number. The raised dot is kept for this; × multiplies two numbers.

objects.text: Python: u @ v or np.dot(u, v). Spreadsheet: =SUMPRODUCT(u, v). The cosine slides later link this number to the angle.

slides.notes:
The dot product as a formula is a sigma sum. For each position i from one to d, multiply entry i of u by entry i of v, then add. With our numbers that is one times two, plus two times zero, plus two times one, which is four.

I write the times sign between plain numbers and keep the raised dot for the dot product of two vectors. In Python you write u at v, and in a spreadsheet SUMPRODUCT. Later today the same number turns up again inside cosine similarity.

title.text:
The L2 norm is the length of the
arrow, from the Pythagoras rule

objects.alt: The L2 norm is the length of the arrow, from the Pythagoras rule

objects.text: L2 norm (Euclidean norm): the length of a vector. It is written ‖a‖.

runs.text: The square root of 25 is 5, so ‖a‖ = 5.
A longer arrow has a bigger norm.

slides.notes:
The L2 norm, also called the Euclidean norm, is the length of the arrow. In two dimensions it is the Pythagoras rule you know from school. The arrow for three, four makes a right-angled triangle with sides three and four. Three squared is nine, four squared is sixteen, the total is twenty-five and the square root is five.

The same recipe works for any number of entries: square each entry, add, take the square root. For one, two, two that gives the square root of nine, which is three.

title.text:
The L2 norm is the square root
of a vector dotted with itself

objects.alt: The L2 norm is the square root of a vector dotted with itself

rows.text: The L2 norm. The subscript 2 means squares and a square root.
Add up over the d entries of a.
Entry i of the vector a.
The dot product of a with itself: the squared length.

objects.text: Python: np.linalg.norm(a). Spreadsheet: =SQRT(SUMPRODUCT(a, a)).

slides.notes:
As a formula, the norm says: square every entry, add them, take the square root. The subscript two says we use squares, and that is why it is called the L2 norm. The sum of squares is the dot product of a with itself, so the norm is the square root of a dot a.

For three, four we get five, and for one, two, two we get three. In Python, np dot linalg dot norm does it. In a spreadsheet use SQRT of SUMPRODUCT of the range with itself, which is the formula written in cells.

title.text:
Euclidean distance is the length
of the arrow between two points

objects.alt: Euclidean distance is the length of the arrow between two points

objects.text: Euclidean distance between the points P and R: the L2 norm of their difference, R − P.

runs.text: R − P = (3, 4), so the distance is 5.
A small distance means the two rows are close, so they are alike.

slides.notes:
To measure how far apart two points are, subtract them and take the norm of the difference. Take the point P equals one, one and the point R equals four, five. The difference is three, four, and we already know its length is five. This is the Euclidean distance.

If each row of a table is a point, the distance tells you how alike two rows are. A small distance means similar, which is how you might find customers who look like a given customer.

title.text:
Distance subtracts entry by entry,
squares, adds and takes the root

objects.alt: Distance subtracts entry by entry, squares, adds and takes the root

rows.text: Two points, each written as a vector with d entries.
Entry i of P and of R.
Add up over the d entries.
The distance: the length of the arrow from P to R.

objects.text: Python: np.linalg.norm(R - P). Spreadsheet: =SQRT(SUMXMY2(P, R)). The letter q is kept for the query vector.

slides.notes:
The distance formula has four moves. Subtract the two points entry by entry, square every difference, add them up and take the square root. That is the L2 norm of the difference. With P equal to one, one and R equal to four, five, the differences are three and four, the squares are nine and sixteen, and the root of twenty-five is five.

I call the points P and R, because the letter q is kept for the query vector that we meet in the search. In Python you write the norm of R minus P. Swapping P and R changes every sign, but the squares remove the signs, so the distance is the same.

title.text:
The cosine of an angle tells how far an arrow
of length 1 reaches along the horizontal

objects.alt: The cosine of an angle tells how far an arrow of length 1 reaches along the horizontal

objects.text: Trigonometry refresher. θ (theta) is an angle. An arrow of length 1 at angle θ reaches cos θ sideways.

runs.text: arccos goes back to the angle: ACOS, np.arccos.
Computers give radians: 180° = π ≈ 3.142. DEGREES() or np.degrees() converts.

slides.notes:
Cosine similarity needs one idea from trigonometry, so here it is from the start. Take an angle theta between two arrows. Draw an arrow of length one at that angle. How far it reaches along the horizontal is the cosine of theta. At sixty degrees it reaches halfway, so cos sixty degrees is zero point five.

Straight along, it reaches one. Straight up, zero. Pointing backwards, minus one. Going back from a cosine to its angle is called arccos, ACOS in a spreadsheet. One trap: computers measure angles in radians, where one hundred and eighty degrees is pi, about three point one four, so you convert with DEGREES.

title.text:
Cosine similarity compares directions
and ignores the lengths of the vectors

objects.alt: Cosine similarity compares directions and ignores the lengths of the vectors

objects.text: Cosine similarity: the cosine of the angle θ between two vectors.

runs.text: Angles are measured from the horizontal arrow (cosine 1).
Same direction: 1. At right angles: 0. Opposite directions: −1.
The lengths do not matter.

slides.notes:
Cosine similarity is the cosine of the angle between two vectors, the idea from the last slide. For the same direction the angle is zero and the cosine is one. At a right angle the cosine is zero. For opposite directions it is minus one. Because it only looks at the angle, the lengths of the vectors do not change the result.

A vector that is long for any reason, a scaling quirk or a very common text, cannot win on length alone. Which is more alike, an angle of ten degrees or an angle of eighty?

title.text:
Divide the dot product by both
lengths and the cosine is left

objects.alt: Divide the dot product by both lengths and the cosine is left

rows.text: The L2 norms of the two vectors.
The angle between the arrows. arccos undoes cosine.

objects.text: Angle: np.degrees(np.arccos(cos)) or =DEGREES(ACOS(cos)). ACOS alone gives radians.

slides.notes:
Cosine similarity is the dot product divided by the product of the two lengths. Turned around, the dot product equals length times length times the cosine, which is why it measures alignment. For a equals three four and b equals four three, the dot product is twenty-four, and both lengths are five, so the cosine is zero point nine six and the angle is about sixteen point three degrees.

For u and v from the dot product slide, four over three times two point two three six gives zero point five nine six, an angle of fifty-three degrees. The cosine can never go above one.

title.text:
Distance and cosine similarity
answer different questions

objects.text: Euclidean distance

runs.text: Compares positions.
a = (3, 4) and 2a = (6, 8): distance 5.
Small means similar.

objects.text: Cosine similarity

runs.text: Compares directions.
The same two vectors: cosine 1.
Large means similar.

objects.text: A vector stretched for any reason keeps its cosine but moves away in distance.

slides.notes:
Distance and cosine answer different questions. Take a equals three, four and two a equals six, eight. The second vector is the first stretched to twice the length. The distance between them is five, which sounds far apart. The cosine similarity is exactly one, because they point the same way.

For our six sentences the two measures happen to pick the same top four, so the choice will not change today's search. It matters when lengths differ for reasons unrelated to meaning, and the lab stretches one vector to show it. For two customers compared by age and spend, distance is often the better choice.

title.text:
Common mistake: trusting the
biggest dot product as the best match

objects.text: Wrong

runs.text: The largest dot product is the closest match.
A vector 10 times longer scores 10 times higher.

objects.text: Right

runs.text: Divide by both lengths first: that is cosine similarity.
Lab: picnic vector × 20. Dot product 1.6 beats 0.785; cosine stays 0.097.

objects.text: Normalising scales every vector to length 1 (a unit vector). Then dot product equals cosine.

slides.notes:
A common mistake is to rank by the raw dot product. The dot product grows with the lengths. If you multiply a vector by ten, all its dot products grow by ten, even though it points the same way. So a long vector can jump to the top of the ranking for no good reason.

Dividing by both lengths removes that effect, and the result is the cosine similarity. In the lab you stretch the picnic vector by twenty, and its dot product of one point six beats zero point seven eight five. Many embedding models scale every vector to length one, called normalising, and then the dot product equals the cosine.

Attention in Session 18 uses a raw dot product scaled by a fixed number, so the raw dot product has its place.

title.text: An embedding turns a piece of text into a vector

objects.alt: An embedding turns a piece of text into a vector

objects.text: An embedding is a vector that represents text, so that similar meanings get similar vectors.

runs.text: Each row is one short sentence with d = 4 numbers.
These numbers are illustrative (made-up numbers). Real embeddings have hundreds of numbers.

slides.notes:
An embedding is a vector that represents a piece of text, so that texts with similar meaning get similar vectors. Here are six short sentences, each with four numbers. These numbers are made up to show the arithmetic. Look at the first two rows. Both are about passwords, and their numbers are similar.

The refund sentences are similar to each other too, and different from the password ones. In a real system a trained model produces the numbers, there are hundreds of them per text, and no single number has a name. Ranking by cosine similarity finds which sentence is closest to a question.

title.text:
Ranking by cosine similarity finds
the sentence closest to the query

objects.alt: Ranking by cosine similarity finds the sentence closest to the query

objects.text: The query is also turned into a vector: (0.85, 0.15, 0.05, 0.05). Compare it with every sentence.

runs.text: S1 and S2, the password sentences, score 0.995 and 0.994.
The picnic and opening hours score below 0.1.

slides.notes:
The search itself is short. The query, I forgot my password, is turned into a vector with the same four numbers. We compute the cosine similarity between the query and every sentence, and sort. The two password sentences come out on top, with zero point nine nine five and zero point nine nine four.

The refund sentences are in the middle, and the picnic and opening hours are near zero. The system returns the top sentence or the top few. In the lab you do exactly this, and you can check every number. The top two are close because both are about passwords.

runs.text: dot = np.sum(u * v)
norm_a = np.sqrt(np.sum(a * a))
cos = a @ b / (norm_a * norm_b)
norms = np.linalg.norm(E, axis=1)

sims = E @ q / (norms * norm_q)

objects.text: In plain words

runs.text: Line 1: dot product. Spreadsheet: SUMPRODUCT.
Line 2: L2 norm. Spreadsheet: SQRT(SUMPRODUCT(a, a)).
Line 3: cosine of a and b.
Lines 4 to 6: one norm per row of E (axis=1), the norm of q, all six cosines.
Line 7: position of the largest. Spreadsheet: =INDEX(A4:A9, MATCH(MAX(H4:H9), H4:H9, 0)).

slides.notes:
Read the recipe before the lab. Line one is the dot product as a sum of products. Line two is the norm, the square root of a vector dotted with itself. Line three is cosine similarity for two vectors. Line four finds one norm per row of E, because axis equals one means go along each row, and line five finds the norm of the query.

Line six gives all six cosines at once. Line seven finds the position of the biggest value. In a spreadsheet, MAX finds the biggest cosine, MATCH finds its row, and INDEX reads the sentence in that row. With a thousand sentences, no line would change.

title.text:
Four messages you may meet,
what they mean and what to do

rows.text: ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together
You combined two vectors with different numbers of entries.
Print a.shape and b.shape. They must match.
A division is missing, or the wrong norm was used.
Divide by both norms, each from its own vector.
The two ranges in SUMPRODUCT have different sizes.
Select ranges with the same number of cells.

slides.notes: Four messages you may meet. A value error about broadcasting means two vectors have different numbers of entries, so print the shapes. A cosine above one means a division is missing. Hash VALUE in a spreadsheet usually means two ranges of different sizes. And an angle of zero point two eight four is the right angle in radians, so convert it to degrees. Read the message first, because it usually tells you the answer.

title.text:
Where this appears in AI:
finding the right passage

objects.alt: Where this appears in AI: finding the right passage

objects.text: RAG (Lewis et al., 2020) scores by dot product; for length-1 vectors that is the cosine.

slides.notes:
When an assistant searches your documents, the common design is this. Your question is turned into an embedding. The passages in your documents have been turned into embeddings earlier and stored. The system scores the question against every passage, takes the highest few, and gives them to the language model, which writes the answer.

Published research calls this retrieval-augmented generation. The 2020 paper scores by a dot product, and many search tools normalise vectors to length one first, which makes it the cosine. Several vendors publish embedding services that return a vector for text you send, but how a given assistant searches inside is not published, so I only describe the standard published pattern.

Open embedding models publish their size, for example 768 numbers per text for BERT base. Our four numbers are a toy version, and the gold step is the one you just built.

Where this appears in AI: check
an assistant with your numbers

runs.text: Use only public maths. Never paste confidential data.

objects.text: You keep
A note: the assistant answer, your lab number, and whether they agree.

slides.notes:
A short activity. Open any AI assistant you like and ask it for the cosine similarity of three four and four three. Compare its answer with your lab number, zero point nine six. Then ask it to show the dot product and both lengths, and check them against twenty-four, five and five.

Ask for the angle too. Did it get everything right?

Never paste confidential data into an assistant. These numbers are public maths, so they are safe. Write down what you found, and keep it for the exit check.

10, because 36 + 64 = 100 and the square root of 100 is 10.
When is ranking by the raw dot product risky, and what fixes it?
When vector lengths differ: a long vector can win on length alone. Divide by both lengths (cosine), or normalise every vector to length 1 first.
